summary: Describes the techniques and mechanisms currently used to allocate and assign IP multicast addresses. Documentation had fallen out of date and this caused confusion, so this informational memo gives an overview of the multicast addressing architecture as it stood at the time.

eli5.summary: Multicast is like a radio broadcast many can tune into, and each station needs its own channel number. This explains how those channel numbers are handed out and who decides.

questions: difference between multicast allocation and assignment
subtitle: A map of how IP multicast addresses are allocated to networks and assigned to applications.

tldr.problem: Documentation on IP multicast address allocation and assignment was out of date and confusing, and RFC 2908 was misleading on the subject.
tldr.mechanism: The memo separates allocation (how operators get large blocks) from assignment (how applications get an address), then surveys each technique for IPv4 and IPv6 and says which are really used.
tldr.outcome: It concludes that derived and unicast-prefix-based allocation work well, manual and static assignment are typical, and dynamic allocation protocols were abandoned or never widely deployed. It obsoletes RFC 2908.

today: RFC 6308 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 2908. No later RFC is listed as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why This Overview Exists
sections.content:
Good, up-to-date documentation of IP multicast addressing was close to non-existent, and some of it was confusing or misleading, notably RFC 2908. RFC 6308 gives a brief overview of the techniques, which it informally calls the multicast addressing architecture.

It focuses on Any Source Multicast (ASM). Source-Specific Multicast does not have these problems, because SSM group addresses have only local significance. The memo obsoletes RFC 2908 and reclassifies it, along with RFC 2776 and RFC 2909, as Historic.
sections.eli5: The old instructions for picking multicast channel numbers were confusing, so this memo replaces them with a clear guide.

sections.title: Allocation Versus Assignment
sections.content:
Earlier multicast documents used "allocation" and "assignment" interchangeably. Address management communities do not. In this memo, allocation describes how network operators obtain larger blocks of addresses, and assignment describes how applications, nodes or sets of nodes obtain a multicast address for their use.

This mirrors unicast practice, where IANA leases big blocks to Regional Internet Registries, and smaller blocks or single addresses go to end sites or users.
sections.eli5: Allocation is a school getting a whole range of locker numbers. Assignment is each student being told which locker is theirs.

sections.title: Allocation: Getting a Block of Addresses
sections.content:
Derived allocation computes a block from something the operator already has. GLOP (RFC 3180) puts the 16-bit public AS number in the middle of the IPv4 prefix 233.0.0.0/8, giving each AS a /24; for example AS 5662 maps to 233.22.30.0/24. It does not work with 4-byte AS numbers, and was never defined for IPv6. For IPv6, RFC 3306 embeds up to 64 high-order bits of a unicast prefix in the multicast address, leaving at least 32 bits of group-id space.

Administratively scoped allocation uses 239.0.0.0/8 in IPv4, divided into Local Scope (239.255.0.0/16) and Organization Local Scope (239.192.0.0/14), or a 4-bit scope field in IPv6. It suits groups inside one administration but is awkward for groups shared across routing domains.

Static IANA allocation of up to 256 addresses is rare, and the RFC prefers other means when available. IANA can allocate from "AD-HOC Block III" (formerly EGLOP), especially for holders of 32-bit AS numbers.

Dynamic allocation protocols such as MASC and AAP were complex and never deployed or seriously implemented. The memo concludes they give no benefit beyond GLOP and unicast-prefix-based mechanisms and have been abandoned.
sections.eli5: A network can get its block of channel numbers by working them out from a number it already owns, by using a shared local range, or by asking the central office. Fancy automatic ordering systems were invented but nobody used them.

sections.title: Assignment: Getting an Address for an Application
sections.content:
Derived assignment exists only for IPv6 link-scoped multicast, where the EUI64 is embedded in the address. Manual assignment means asking the network operator, by phone or email, for an address and configuring it by hand. It works when groups are small, and is the most commonly used technique when an application has no static IANA assignment.

Static IANA assignment comes in two forms. A global assignment is simplest for developers, who can hard-code the address, but it encourages a "land-grab" of the limited address space. A scope-relative assignment is an offset from the highest address in each IPv4 administrative scope: the SLPv2 discovery offset is 2, giving 239.255.255.253 in Local Scope and 239.195.255.253 in Organization Local Scope.

Dynamic assignment protocols such as MADCAP and the Session Announcement Protocol exist, but only a few implemented MADCAP, and creating a session with SAP is tedious. The memo says more work on rendezvous and service discovery would be needed to make dynamic assignment more useful.
sections.eli5: An app can ask a person for a channel number, use a number reserved for it in advance, or ask a computer to hand one out. Asking a person and reserved numbers are what almost everyone does.

sections.title: Summary and Future Work
sections.content:
For IPv4, GLOP is sufficient for those with 16-bit AS numbers, and IANA allocates from AD-HOC Block III for 32-bit AS number holders. For IPv6, unicast-prefix-based addresses and their derivatives are a good strategy, and also work for scoped addresses. The memo calls dynamic allocation too complex and unnecessary, and notes that manual assignment is typical today.

Suggested future actions: analyze multicast address discovery and rendezvous in more depth, consider more IPv4 administratively scoped ranges for applications that should not be routed over the Internet, and consider a stricter policy such as "IETF Consensus" for static IANA allocations.

The memo says it has no security considerations of its own, and that analysis of the mentioned protocols is out of scope.
sections.eli5: The guide says the simple, number-based ways work best, and the complicated automatic systems were not worth it.
